To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the reduction of urban nutrients inputs leads to a rapid and complete recovery of coastal lagoons, (ii) recovery trajectories are dependent of the initial status of the lagoon, (iii) the response of coastal lagoon is not a simple linear response, (iv) the response of the lagoon may be delayed by the presence of a large reservoir of TP in the sediment and (v) the response of phytoplanktic biomass is more rapid than the response of nutrients
nutrient reduction in urban wastewater treatment plants can lead to a rapid recovery of coastal lagoons.
the recovery of coastal lagoons from eutrophication depends on the eutrophic status before remediation actions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the recovery trajectories following the remediation of coastal lagoons, a topic of increasing interest in the context of the European WFD.
the recovery trajectories of coastal lagoons and provides a framework for the evaluation of the effectiveness of remediation actions.
the question of the rapidity and extent of the response of coastal lagoons to remediation actions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the recovery of coastal lagoons is possible but requires a long-term monitoring programme.
a 50% reduction of TP loadings is enough to recover the eutrophic state of the lagoon, whereas a 70-80% reduction is necessary for the hypertrophic lagoons.

the recovery trajectories following the remediation of the eutrophic systems are rapid, complete, but that the recovery of the hypertrophic systems is slower, less complete, and may include feedbacks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nutrient inputs are not the sole factor that controls phytoplankton dynamics, but that nutrient inputs are a necessary condition to maintain a high phytoplankton biomass.
the reduction in nutrient inputs to the lagoon has a rapid and complete effect on the phytoplankton biomass and the nutrient concentrations.
nutrient remediation can be effective in coastal lagoons, but that the recovery trajectory will vary depending on the eutrophic state of the lagoon and that recovery can take decades.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the recovery trajectories are not necessarily linear and that the eutrophied lagoon can recover rapidly to its natural oligo-mesotrophic state, but that it may also take a much longer time to recover from a hypertrophic state.
the recovery of coastal ecosystems can be rapid, and that remediation of urban nutrient loads can be effective in reducing the eutrophying effects of urban waste waters.
the WFD targets are achievable for eutrophic ecosystems but that they should be adapted to the eutrophic status of the lagoonal ecosystems.
